props.title: The baby shower, the bridal shower, and the one with everybody.

rows.text: An afternoon at home or in a garden, with the guest of honor’s mother and her friends at one end of the table and her own friends at the other. One guitar under the food, and a song for the mother-to-be if there’s one she wants.

A private dining space, a garden or a house, usually a few months before the wedding. A guitarist or a duo plays the standards under lunch, a singer plays the couple’s song if the host wants it, and the same duo can play the cocktail hour on the day, on the same contract.
The evening version on a patio, with partners and friends of both invited, which makes it a small party more than a lunch. A singer with a guitar or a duo plays it, the way it plays a backyard party.

props._notes: The three showers, each with the size that fits. Links ACROSS to the brunch page, the weddings tree and the backyard page. No clock times.

items.q: Can you play live music at a baby shower?
items.a: Yes. Most baby showers book one guitar, a jazz guitarist or a Spanish guitarist playing under the meal, and a singer with a guitar takes the guest of honor's requests where the host wants a voice in the afternoon. It's booked through Signet Artists in Denver.

items.q: How loud is it, and how much space does it need?
items.a: About the level of the conversation at the table, so grandmothers and friends hear each other across it. One guitar takes about 6 by 4 feet on one circuit and 45 minutes to set up, and a duo 8 by 6, in the corner of a dining space or under cover in a garden. Sets run 45 to 60 minutes with music through the breaks. A certificate of insurance and a W-9 come with the quote if the venue asks.

items.q: Can the music work outdoors in a garden?
items.a: Yes, under cover and out of direct sun, with power run to it. Where there's no socket, a guitarist can play with a battery-powered system.
